title: Hollis & Vane: the turnaround plan
prompt: Our client is Hollis & Vane, a department-store chain with 120 stores and $2.4B of revenue. After years of drift it is now losing money, its lenders are nervous, and a new CEO has been brought in with a mandate to transform the business. She has asked us to build the turnaround plan: how much the business must improve, where the money will come from, and how to carry an exhausted organisation through it.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 1 — Hollis & Vane, annual figures
exhibits.unitsNote: Store-level EBIT is before head-office costs

exhibits.title: Exhibit 2 — The tail of the store network
exhibits.text: The weakest 20 stores lose an average of $2M a year each at store level, after every reasonable local fix has been tried. Their leases allow exit within the year. Closing a store transfers little of its revenue to other stores in the chain.

exhibits.title: Exhibit 3 — Head-office benchmark
exhibits.text: Comparable retailers run head offices at about 10% of revenue. Hollis & Vane spends $300M — a quarter more than the benchmark implies for its $2.4B of sales.

questions.prompt: Before we build the plan, what should we clarify with the CEO first? Select the two most relevant.
options: What outcome do the lenders and board require, and by when?
How much cash runway does the company have while the plan takes effect?
Which department store the CEO shopped at as a child?
The colour palette of the spring window displays?
Whether the company sponsors a football team?

optionRationale: A turnaround is measured against whatever keeps the lenders committed; the target must come from them, not from ambition.
The clock. A perfect three-year plan is worthless if the cash runs out in eighteen months.
Nostalgia is not a constraint.
Not decision-relevant.
A minor cost line at most; not what to ask with the first question.
commonMistakes: Designing the plan before pinning down the number and the deadline it must hit
Ignoring liquidity — in a turnaround, cash timing outranks accounting profit

questions.followUp:
The lenders will refinance if the plan credibly returns the business to a 5% EBIT margin, and the CEO wants every action launched within her first year.

On cash: runway is tight but sufficient if the plan starts fast — which is why the plan must be built from actions that can begin now.

Here is the business as it stands.

questions.prompt: Which areas would you examine to build the turnaround plan? Select the four most relevant.
options: The store network — which stores make money and which never will
The cost structure above the stores — head office against benchmark
Buying and operating costs — procurement and store productivity
The organisation itself — capability, morale, and who will carry the change
The founder’s original 1908 business plan
Competitors’ staff canteen menus
The chain’s horoscope for the coming year

optionRationale: In a store chain the network is the portfolio; the tail usually hides much of the loss.
Overhead is the cost the customer never sees — the first place a turnaround looks.
The operational levers that improve every store that remains.
The lever that decides whether the others happen: transformations fail on people more than on arithmetic.
A century-old document is not a turnaround input.
Not relevant.
Not analysis.
commonMistakes: Building a plan that is all arithmetic and no organisation
Treating every store as saveable out of sentiment

questions.followUp: We will take them in that order — first the size of the mountain, then the levers.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, how much annual EBIT improvement does the plan need to deliver to reach the lenders’ 5% margin?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Target EBIT: 5% × $2,400M = $120M.
Today: −$60M.
Required improvement: $120M − (−$60M) = $180M a year.
commonMistakes: Answering $120M — forgetting the plan first has to climb out of a $60M hole
Subtracting the loss instead of adding it

questions.followUp: $180M a year — the mountain has a number. Now the levers, starting with the store network.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, how much annual EBIT improvement does closing the 20 weakest stores deliver?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
20 stores × $2M of store-level losses each = $40M a year of losses that stop.
The exhibit rules out the usual objections: local fixes are exhausted, leases allow exit, and little revenue transfers.
commonMistakes: Netting off imagined transferred revenue the exhibit says not to count
Counting closure one-off costs here — they matter for cash, but the question is annual EBIT improvement

questions.followUp: A quarter of the target from simply stopping the worst losses. Next, the cost the customer never sees.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, how much annual saving does bringing head office to the benchmark deliver?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Benchmark: 10% × $2,400M = $240M.
Today: $300M.
Saving: $300M − $240M = $60M a year — a 20% reduction in head-office cost, which in practice means roles, not paperclips.
commonMistakes: Benchmarking against the post-closure revenue base prematurely — the closures barely move $2.4B
Treating the saving as achievable without redundancies, which understates the human weight of the plan

questions.followUp: Now two operating levers, briefly: procurement can save 2.5% of cost of goods sold, and smarter store scheduling can save 5% of store payroll. Put the whole cost programme together.

questions.prompt: Adding the closures, the head-office reduction, the procurement saving and the scheduling saving: how much of the $180M do the four cost levers deliver?
questions.answerFormatNote: Enter in $ millions, rounded to the nearest million.

idealAnswer.workedSolution:
Closures: $40M.
Head office: $60M.
Procurement: 2.5% × $1,440M COGS = $36M.
Scheduling: 5% × $480M payroll = $24M.
Total: $40M + $60M + $36M + $24M = $160M.
commonMistakes: Taking procurement on revenue instead of COGS
Taking scheduling on total payroll including head office, double-counting the overhead cut
Calling $160M close enough — the lenders asked for $180M, and “nearly” does not refinance

questions.followUp: $160M — $20M short. Cost alone does not close a $180M gap, which is the point where weak turnarounds start shaving the truth. Strong ones find the rest somewhere real.

questions.prompt: The plan needs $20M more of annual EBIT. Which two moves would you put in the plan to close the gap? Select the two most credible.
options: Cut the marketing budget by a further $20M
Relaunch the loyalty programme and online store — plans the team already has — adding $100M of revenue at a 20% contribution margin
Raise all prices by 5% across the board
Renegotiate the leases of the retained stores, where terms are above market
Close 40 more stores

optionRationale: Self-defeating: the plan needs revenue to hold while stores close; cutting demand generation to hit a cost number is how turnarounds spiral.
Credible and quantified: $100M × 20% = $20M, built on initiatives the organisation already believes in — which matters for momentum.
A blanket 5% rise on a struggling banner risks accelerating the sales decline that caused the crisis.
Credible: a chain in visible difficulty has real leverage with landlords who do not want 20 more dark stores.
The remaining 100 stores are not the loss-makers; closing profitable stores deepens the hole.
commonMistakes: Closing the gap with a cut that undermines the revenue the plan depends on
Ignoring that “the team already believes in it” is itself a selection criterion in a transformation

questions.followUp:
Agreed on both — the loyalty and online relaunch is the one we will size in the plan: $100M of revenue at 20% contribution closes the $20M exactly, with lease renegotiation held as contingency.

The arithmetic now works. What remains is the part that usually fails: the organisation that has to deliver it.

questions.prompt: This plan closes 20 stores and cuts a fifth of head office. What are the most relevant people and organisation risks to manage? Select the three most relevant.
options: The best people leaving first — top performers have options, and uncertainty sends them to competitors
Middle management overload — the same leaders must run the stores and deliver the change
The office plants dying during the head-office move
Change fatigue and rumour — a year of redundancies corroding the service customers experience
The CEO’s diary being too full

optionRationale: The classic transformation wound: the plan keeps the roles but loses the people who made them work.
Real: every lever lands on the same store and regional managers, and overload turns into missed execution.
Not a risk.
Real and customer-facing: demoralised floors sell less, and the revenue lever depends on stores that still care.
Diary management is not an organisational risk.
commonMistakes: Managing the leavers and ignoring the workload of those who stay
Treating morale as soft while the plan’s revenue line quietly depends on it

questions.followUp:
Retention: identify the critical few hundred people early and lock them in with clarity and, where needed, money.

Overload: sequence the levers rather than launching everything at once, and give the change a dedicated programme team instead of adding it to day jobs.

Fatigue: communicate the whole plan once, honestly — one big announcement beats a year of drip-fed bad news, and it lets the organisation see the credible future it is working toward.

questions.prompt: The CEO presents to the lenders tomorrow and asks you to rehearse the plan with her. Summarise it in seven to eight lines maximum.

keyPoints: Leads with the destination: from a $60M loss to a $120M EBIT — a $180M annual improvement, fully identified
Lists the levers with numbers: closures $40M, head office $60M, procurement $36M, scheduling $24M, loyalty and online relaunch $20M
Notes that every action launches within the first year, which is what the runway requires
Names the people plan as part of the plan, not an appendix: retention of critical staff, sequenced rollout, honest communication
Acknowledges what is hard — 20 closures and a fifth of head office — rather than presenting a painless story
Stays inside seven or eight lines
commonMistakes: Presenting $160M of levers and hoping the lenders do not subtract
Reciting the cost levers and omitting the organisation that must deliver them
Overselling the revenue lever, the plan’s only non-cost line, without its conditions

closing: That is the end of the case. Your transcript is ready — copy it into an LLM to be graded on what you actually said, not on what you meant.
